doc.title: Pierre Boussaguet interviewed by Matthieu Jaffre, Aix en Provence, France, July 28, 2020

title: Johnny Griffin on Lafitte's grand cru tone and distinctive sounds
summary: Griffin tells him it will take ten years to accept another tenor after Lafitte; he reflects on recognizable tones.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: I mean he is in the pure tradition of the great tenor saxophone like Coleman Hawkins, Don Byas, Lucky Thompson, you can really feel the deep sounds in him.

I’ll tell you a story. A few weeks after that, one of the shows that was supposed to be performed with my trio and Johnny Griffin and Guy, of course Guy was just a few days before going to pass away. And I still had that concert to play with Griff. So I remember I was down by his house in the middle of the west part of France. So I go to Griff’s house. And he said, I stayed at his house, and he said, “Okay tomorrow we take my wife’s car and you and I will drive to the concert.” And when we got there we were really in advance like maybe two in the afternoon and sound check was at five. So he says, “Baby, what about a drink?” I said, “Okay.” So we were in a private salon in the hotel and I remember talking about Guy at some point. He said, he said, “Pierre, you have to face a tough period.” I said, “What you mean?” He said, “Well, I know you love first class Bordeaux wine.” He says, “So do I.” He said, “You don’t realize that you’ve been performing for the past ten years with a premier grand cru sound of the saxophone. Because Guy —

So true. A beautiful tone. So he told me he said, “I take a number. It will take you approximately ten years to be able to accept mentally to deal with another tenor saxophonist.” On the spot I said wow, if he tells me so, I remember — but somewhere, no, life has to move on. And in fact that’s the way it happened. And it took me maybe seven, eight, nine hours [years] I didn’t count — but I always — there was one day —
So Johnny Griffin is the one who told you try to bring the —
He told me he said Guy Lafitte is one of the first five premier grand cru, such a beautiful tone.
But the message, the message was that you got used to that. Because every time I played with a tenor there was —

And I must say, I’ve seen that beautiful interview about Sweets, talking about the sound. All these cats, I would say these cats, that’s a word we used, but to me all of these masters, the force — and I’m not a traditionalist, I’m not avante garde.
You know if it’s Johnny Hodges. If we talk about alto you know if it’s Art Pepper. If it’s Phil Woods, Charlie Parker.
Cannonball Adderley. I mean all of them. And with Guy you hear just that one note, it’s not even part of the note he’s playing —
